unit.title: How attacks work, and how to defend

lesson.title: Malware: how it gets in
lesson.subtitle: Five kinds, the doors they use, and how to close them

video.title: Malware: how it gets in
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Computer room after school. Mr Joseph holds up a student's phone covered in pop-up adverts; a game icon with a crown and coins sits on the home screen.
scenes.animation: Pop-ups multiply on the phone screen; Joseph raises an eyebrow at the camera.
scenes.narration: “Free coins, and every level unlocked!” That’s what a modded game promised one of my students. A week later, his phone was full of pop-ups and his data bundle had vanished. Free turned out to be expensive.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card: the Darsi mark, the lesson title and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how malware gets onto phones and computers, and how you keep it out.

scenes.visual: A phone in the middle; four small icons orbit it: a key, an eye, a megaphone, a padlock.
scenes.animation: Icons appear one by one as they are named.
scenes.narration: Malware means malicious software: any program made to harm a device or the person using it. It can steal your passwords, watch what you type, flood you with adverts, or lock your files and demand money.

scenes.visual: Five rows, each with an icon and the name of a kind of malware.
scenes.animation: Rows slide in as each kind is named.
scenes.narration: There are a few main kinds. A virus hides in a file and spreads when it’s shared. A worm spreads by itself across a network. A trojan pretends to be useful, like a free game hack. Ransomware locks your files and demands payment. Spyware quietly watches what you do.

scenes.visual: Four doors into a house-shaped phone: a game with a crown, a USB stick, an envelope with a paperclip, a red alert box.
scenes.animation: Each door opens as it is named.
scenes.narration: Surprisingly, most malware doesn’t break in. It’s invited. Modded apps and cracked games from outside the official store. A USB stick passed around at the cyber café. An attachment you weren’t expecting. And fake alerts that shout, “Your phone has three viruses!”

scenes.visual: A stranger at a front door holds out a shiny gift box. A teenager carries it inside; the box's shadow is a wooden horse.
scenes.animation: Door opens; the box crosses the doorway; the horse shadow fades in.
scenes.narration: It’s like a stranger at your door with a beautiful gift box. Malware rarely smashes a window: usually, you carry the box in yourself. That’s why one kind is named after the Trojan horse.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds up her phone: a red pop-up with a big warning triangle and an Install button. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Salma slides in; the cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A website suddenly says my phone has three viruses and tells me to install a cleaner now. What should I do?

scenes.visual: The ‘close the page’ card gets a check badge; the pop-up shrinks and disappears; the phone's own shield icon glows.
scenes.on_screen_text: Close it: the alert is fake
scenes.narration: Close the page. A website can’t look inside your phone, so the alert is fake, and the “cleaner” is often the malware itself. If you’re worried, open your phone’s own protection yourself.

scenes.visual: Four shields in a row, each with an icon: arrows going round, a checked store bag, a scanner, a stack of copies.
scenes.animation: Shields lock into place one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: Four defences, and why they work
scenes.narration: Now the defences, and why they work. Updates close the holes malware uses. Official stores check apps before you get them. Built-in protection scans what you install. And a backup means even ransomware can’t take your work.

scenes.visual: A phone with four warning symptoms: a draining battery, adverts, an unknown app icon, a data meter falling to zero.
scenes.animation: Each symptom appears as it is named.
scenes.narration: How would you know? The battery drains much faster than usual. Adverts pop up everywhere. There’s an app you don’t remember installing. Or your data bundle vanishes overnight.

scenes.visual: Four numbered steps: Wi-Fi switching off, a student talking to Mr Joseph, a second clean laptop, a restore arrow.
scenes.narration: Think a device is infected? Turn off Wi-Fi and mobile data, so it can’t spread. Tell your IT teacher or an adult at home. Change important passwords on a clean device. Then remove the app, or restore from a backup.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds a USB stick labelled with a game controller. Two answer cards bounce in: a check and a warning triangle.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Your cousin offers you a cracked copy of a paid game on a USB stick. It’s free, and it’s from family. Do you install it?

scenes.visual: The ‘no’ card gets the check badge. Four summary cards line up: a store bag, update arrows, a backup stack, a raised hand.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: No: cracked games are one of the easiest ways in for malware, even from family. Remember: apps only from the official store, everything updated, a backup kept, and if something feels wrong, disconnect and tell someone.

scenes.visual: A student at home opens Settings on a phone; a toggle labelled with update arrows switches on. End card: the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Toggle switches on; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: open your phone’s settings and check two things. Are automatic updates on? And is there an app you don’t recognise? On a shared family phone, ask an adult before you remove anything.

checkpoints.prompt: A website pops up: “Your phone has 3 viruses! Install this cleaner now.” What should you do?

options.text: Close the page: the alert is fake
Call the support number in the alert

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a website can’t scan your phone. The alert is fake, and the “cleaner” is often the malware.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a website can’t see inside your phone. The alert, the cleaner and the number all belong to the scammer. Close the page.

checkpoints.prompt: Your cousin offers you a cracked copy of a paid game on a USB stick. Do you install it?

options.text: Yes — it’s from family, so it’s safe
No — cracked games often hide malware

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — cracked software is one of the easiest ways in for malware, even when the person sharing it means well.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — your cousin may mean well, but cracked games often carry malware nobody can see. Get games from the official store.
